Rabi Shankar Chakraborty Advocates with SC Das— For the Petitioner. 
Sirajul Islam Mondal, Advocate — For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Sudhan Chandra Roy  ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Md. Hanif  ----- opposite Party
full_judgment:
2. The opposite party Mr. Hanif as plaintiff instituted SCC Suit No.12 of 1991 in the 3rd Court of Assistant Judge and SCC Court, Dhaka against the defendant-petitioner Sree Sudhan Chandra Ray for eviction. The case of the plaintiff, in brief is that the suit premises as described in the plaint originally belonged to Mrs. Amena Begum and after her death her son, the plaintiff became the owner thereof by registered partition deed between the co-sharers. The plaintiff's mother Amena Begum let out the suit premises to Naz Jewellers as a monthly ejectable tenant before liberation war of Bangladesh and after liberation, during the lifetime of plaintiff's mother the defendant took possession of the suit premises forcefully driving away the owner of Naz Jewellers and started Jewellery business therein and ultimately Mrs. Amena Begum admitted the defendant as a monthly ejectable bharatia in respect of the suit house. Defendant thus became a monthly bharatia under Mrs. Amena Begum and after her death under the plaintiff at a monthly rental of Taka 300.00 The defendant irregularly paid rent to the plaintiff upto March, 1991 and received the rent receipts, but he stopped payment of rent since the month of March, 1991. The defendant is a defaulter and became an undesirable tenant by his behaviour. The plaintiff-landlord also bonafide requires the suit house for his own use and occupation to accommodate his 4 grown up sons therein. Therefore, the plaintiff-landlord served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on 2.7.91 upon the defendant determining his tenancy in respect of the suit house on the expiry of 31st July, 1991. The notice was received by the defendant by putting his signature on 4.7.91 but the defendant did not vacate the suit house after expiry of notice period and, as such, the plaintiff filed the SCC Suit as aforesaid. 

 3. The defendant-tenant contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that the notices under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act served upon the defendant is not valid nor sufficient, that the plaintiff does not bonafide require the suit house as claimed by him. The defendant's further case is that one Aminul Huq purchased the possessory right of the suit house from Mrs. Amina Bibi, the original owner of the suit premises and started jewellery business there. Aminul Hoque paid monthly rent at a rate of Taka 100.00 to the landlady and thereafter he transferred his possession of the suit premises to the defendant and then the defendant became bharatia under the landlady Mrs. Amena Begum at a monthly rent of Taka 100.00 which was subsequently increased to Taka 300.00 The defendant paid rent regularly to the plaintiff and obtained receipt from him. The defendant paid rent to the plaintiff for the month of March, 1991 on 1.4.1991 and the plaintiff granted rent receipt on 7.4.1991 and thereafter the defendant paid rent for the month of April, 1991 to the plaintiff in presence of witness Narayan Chandra Roy and others but that the plaintiff did not give the rent receipt to the defendant. Then again the defendant offered rent to the plaintiff for the month of May, 1991 on 2.6.1991 but the plaintiff did not accept the same. Thereafter, the defendant filed House Rent Control Case No. 37 of 1991 in the Court of House Rent Controller for deposit of rent and that the defendant filed another HR Case No. 36 of 1991 under section 27 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance for rent receipt. Thus the defendant is not a defaulter. The plaintiff's suit is therefore liable to be dismissed. 

 12. By a perusal of the tenant's portion of the rent receipts as filed by the defendant in the suit and the counterfoil as filed by the plaintiff as per Exhibit-7 series, it appears that the defendant Sree Sudhan Chandra Roy was described there in printed forms as an ejectable tenant at will in all the receipts. From all the above documentary, oral evidence of the PWs and DWs it clearly appears that the defendant-petitioner is a monthly ejectable tenant in respect of the suit shop-room. I am, therefore, of the opinion that the learned SCC Judge is quite justified in holding that the defendant is a monthly ejectable tenant under the plaintiff. Thus I find that 15 days notice is sufficient to determine his bharatia right. 

 13. Next question is whether the defendant is a defaulter. It has been seriously contended on behalf of the defendant that the defendant has paid rent to the plaintiff for the month of April 1991 but he refused to accept it and then the defendant filed HR Case No. 37 of 1991 and has been depositing the rent in Court of the House Rent Controller under section 19 of the House Rent Control Ordinance. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party has, on this point, argued that the defendant obtained rent receipts from the plaintiff-landlord on the first day of every month on payment or without payment of the rent but that the defendant could not produce any rent receipt showing payment of rent for April 1991 as because the defendant stopped payment of rent to the plaintiff-landlord from the month of April 1991. 

 14. By a perusal of the impugned Judgment, it appears that the learned SCC Judge framed a separate issue to the effect whether the defendant is a defaulter in respect of payment of rent and after discussing all the facts and evidence of the case with reference to oral and documentary evidence produced by the plaintiff and defendant, the learned SCC Judge has come to a definite finding that the defendant is a defaulter in respect of payment of rent for the month of April 1991 and for the month of January and February, 1992. Defendant's claim is that he paid rent for the month of April, 1991 in presence of witness Narayan Chandra Roy but that the plaintiff did not give him any receipt. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff argued that there was no witness in payment of rent of any of the previous months and so, the question of presence of witness Narayan Ohandra for the month of April only does not arise. 

 15. In appears that the defendant obtained rent receipts on the first day of every month showing payment of rent to the plaintiff as per Ext. 7 series. So the question of non-granting of rent receipt for the month of April, 1991 only by the plaintiff does not arise and this solitary allegation is not a believable allegation. The statement of DW 2 Narayan Chandra Roy that he was present in payment of rent of April, 1991 has not been believed by the learned SCC Judge giving his reasons therein. This DW 2 said in his cross-examination that he was not present in the payment of rent for the month of March, 91 and that the defendant did not pay any rent to the plaintiff for any other month excepting the month of April 1991 in his presence. In the facts and circumstances of the case, the solitary presence of DW 2 Narayan Chandra Roy for the month of April only speaks volumes about the conduct of the defendant towards the plaintiff. For all these reasons and for many other reasons, I find that the learned SCC Judge has rightly disbelieved the statement of DW 2. 

 16. By a detailed discussion of all the above facts, circumstances and evidences of the case, the learned SCC Judge found the defendant-petitioner to be a defaulter in respect of payment of rent for the month of April, 1991 and January, 1992 as because the defendant could not produce any Challan showing deposit of rent for January 92. To this point, the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioner today filed an information slip claiming that the defendant has deposited rent for the month of January and February, 1992. By a perusal of this slip paper, it appears that he had filed a searching only on 7.6.95 in the Judge's Court and got the reply on 8.6.95 But the hearing of this Revision Case was concluded on 6.6.95 when it was found that the learned SCC Judge came to a clear finding that the defendant did not pay any rent for April 1991 and January. 1992 as because he did not file any chalan in Court showing deposit of rent for January, 1992 It may be mentioned here that all the chalans filed by the defendant in the trial Court showing deposit of rent as per HR Case No. 37 of 1991 vide Exhibit 'Kha' Series are all in origin. This copy of chalan with the 'receiving seal' of the Bangladesh Bank is the depositor's copy for each month with a deposit number in seal given by the Treasury in the top of the chalan. But no explanation is given in the Revisional Application or in the affidavit-in-reply against the  counter-affidavit of the opposite party as to what happened to his original chalan of January and February 1992 although he could file the chalans in original form upto December; 91 No. explanation is given during argument also. It is not the case that defendant has lost his chalan for the month of January and February, 1992. The information slip in question as filed today without any petition did not also contain any deposit number of treasury nor of serial number of deposit Register of the Court. There is a difference between chalan Register and deposit Register. For all these reasons this kind of information slip beyond the record cannot be given any credence. 

 17. Under all the above facts and circumstances and evidence on record, I am of the opinion that the clear finding arrived at by the learned SCC Judge in respect of separate issue No. 3 to the effect that defendant is defaulter in respect of payment of rent for the month of April, 1991 and January 1992 is a correct finding based on detailed discussion and proper appreciation of the facts, evidence and materials on record. I therefore find that the learned SCC Judge is quite justified in coming to this decision that the defendant petitioner is a defaulter in payment of rent to the plaintiff-landlord. 

 20. It has been argued on behalf of the defendant-petitioner that the defendant filed a case being HR Case No. 36 of 1991 section 27 of the Rent Control Ordinance for non-issue of rent receipt for the month of April, 1991 which is pending till today. It is contended that the HR Case No. 36 of 1991 should have been disposed of before the SCC Suit No. 12 of 1991. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred to a decision in the case of Narayan Prosad Bhowmik vs. Sree Sree Juktaswar Radha Madhab Jew Thakur Bigraha reported in 40 DLR (HC) 449 wherein it has been observed that non-disposal of the application under section 27 of the Ordinance before the disposal of the present case would render that suit infructuous. To this point, the learned advocates for the plaintiff-opposite party submits that in the instant case the defendant-petitioner became a defaulter in respect of payment of rent in the month of April, 1991 and that on the ground of bonafide requirement and for non payment of rent the plaintiff served a notice upon the defendant under section 106 of the Transfer or Property Act, issued on 2nd July, 1991 and received by him on 4th July, 1991 and immediately thereafter he filed the HR Case No. 36 of 1991 on 6th July 1991 under section 27 of the Rent Control Ordinance which is a penal section and then the defendant filed HR Case No. 37 of 1991 for deposit of rent under section 19 of the Rent Control Ordinance. From the facts and materials on record, it appears that the defendant immediately after receiving the legal notice under section 106 of the TP Act on 4.7.91 has filed both the HR Case No. 36 of 1991 under penal section and HR Case No. 37 of 1991 under section 19 of the Rent Control Ordinance as an attempt to defeat the plaintiff's suit for eviction. Therefore, the facts and circumstances of the instant case are quite different and distinguishable from those of the above cited case. 

 21. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party by referring to exhibit 10 together with enclosed, Exhibit 10 A has said that the defendant-petitioner has not only filed HR Case No. 37 of 1991 against the plaintiff but also he has served two notices as per Exhibits 10 and 10A through Sarna Shilpik Srami Sanga claiming an unfounded amount of Taka 45,000.00 from the plaintiff. It appears from all these papers that the defendant-petitioner has not only filed two House Rent cases, one under a penal section, but also he has got 2 notices issued from Dhaka Sarno Shilpik Srami Samity asking him to appear before them with his documents for hearing in respect of loan money. Sarno Shilpi Sanga issued notices Ext. 10 & 11 in a manner as if they will sit upon him like a Court for hearing the alleged matter. The Sarno Shilpi Sanga has no right to issue such notices upon the plaintiff who is the owner of the suit house. In such facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the opinion that the defendant-petitioner is an undesirable tenant as alleged by the plaintiff in the plaint.
